clue.text: Large drink accepted? One rule for us, another for them!

definitions.text: One rule for us, another for them

blocks.note: a double is a twice-sized measure of spirits
standard means normal, generally accepted

explanation.surface: Someone orders a large drink and, when it is accepted, grumbles that rules differ for others.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark ends the wordplay; the exclamation is the definition, a complaint about unequal treatment.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names a principle applied unfairly, more strictly to one group than to another.

clue.text: Spoilsport wanting party spirit needs them to wind up

blocks.note: a do is a party
gin is a spirit
taken as written
to wind someone up is to annoy them

explanation.surface: A killjoy at a party demands drink and sets out to irritate everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: Wind up is British slang for deliberately annoying someone.
explanation.definitionFit: From Aesop's fable, the phrase describes a person who selfishly stops others enjoying what they cannot use themselves.

clue.text: Nuts lie awkwardly in the saucepan, perhaps

indicators.note: lying awkwardly means sprawled out of order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Some nuts have been dropped clumsily into a cooking pot.
explanation.definitionFit: A saucepan is one example of a kitchen implement, hence 'perhaps'.

clue.text: Runaway win with toboggan

definitions.note: verb read whimsically as 'slide over land'; the answer is a noun

blocks.note: first meaning: an overwhelming victory, especially in an election
second meaning, playful: a slide down the ground, as on a sledge

explanation.surface: A sledging race is won by a huge margin.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is cheeky: tobogganing is literally sliding over land.
explanation.definitionFit: An election rout is called a landslide, and a mass of earth sliding downhill bears the same name.

clue.text: Far Eastern impudence?

blocks.note: surface reading: cheekiness of an Asian kind
setter's reading: sauce means cheek, and here it is a condiment from East Asian cooking

explanation.surface: A question about rudeness from somewhere in the Far East.
explanation.walkthrough: Sauce in British English also means cheek or impudence, so the clue is really a condiment.
explanation.definitionFit: The salty bean-based condiment is a staple of Chinese and Japanese cooking, and its second word also means cheek.

clue.text: Sci-fi author has rewritten "Sal and Sid"

indicators.note: rewriting the names produces a fresh arrangement of their letters

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A science-fiction writer has reworked a story about two characters called Sal and Sid.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the two names are shuffled; 'and' simply joins them.
explanation.definitionFit: Brian Aldiss was a British science-fiction novelist, author of Hothouse.

clue.text: Critical uncle's type of courage?

definitions.note: the answer is the adjective in 'Dutch uncle'
the answer is the adjective in 'Dutch courage'

blocks.note: first meaning: a ... uncle gives blunt, stern advice
second meaning: ... courage is bravery that comes from drink

explanation.surface: Asking what kind of bravery a fault-finding relative has.
explanation.walkthrough: Both are fixed English phrases using the same nationality word.
explanation.definitionFit: The nationality adjective completes both idioms: a stern adviser and alcohol-fuelled boldness.

clue.text: Again intrude inside green territory

indicators.note: inside says the letters sit within the following words

blocks.note: the run of letters straddling the two words

explanation.surface: Someone trespasses again onto a patch of green land.
explanation.definitionFit: To intrude again is to go back in, to come into a place a second time.

clue.text: Speedy way to tie a knot?

definitions.text: Speedy way to tie a knot?

blocks.clueFragment: Speedy way to tie a knot?
blocks.note: surface reading: a quick method of knotting a rope
setter's reading: tying the knot is getting married, and this permit lets it happen without the usual waiting period

explanation.surface: Asking for a quick way to knot string or rope.
explanation.walkthrough: In England and Wales this licence lets a couple marry without the usual notice period of banns.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an official permission allowing a wedding at short notice, so a fast route to marriage.

clue.text: Immature and regarded as jealous

blocks.note: green means inexperienced, unripe
to eye is to look at

explanation.surface: A youngster is seen by others as envious.
explanation.definitionFit: Envy is proverbially the green-eyed monster, from Othello, so the compound describes resentful envy.

clue.text: Contemptible person, one leaving Antwerp

indicators.note: something that leaves is taken away from the word it was in

blocks.note: an is the indefinite article, meaning one
the Belgian port, taken as written

explanation.surface: A despised individual departs from the Belgian city.
explanation.definitionFit: A twerp is a silly, irritating, contemptible person, a mild British insult.

clue.text: Bills for rackets I dropped

indicators.note: dropped means let go, so that letter falls out of the word

blocks.note: a racket is a loud noise
taken as written

explanation.surface: Invoices for tennis equipment, with one item crossed off.
explanation.walkthrough: Bills looks like invoices; it means birds' beaks.
explanation.definitionFit: A bird's bill is its beak, which serves it as a nose would, so beaks may loosely be called noses.

clue.text: Cultured Esther nearly gripped by a muscular movement

indicators.note: nearly means not quite all, so the name loses its final letter
something gripped is held inside whatever grips it

blocks.note: taken as written
the name, taken as written before shortening
a tic is an involuntary twitch of a muscle

explanation.surface: A refined woman called Esther is almost seized by a spasm.
explanation.definitionFit: Aesthetic as an adjective means concerned with beauty and refined taste, so a cultured, artistic sensibility.

clue.text: Steal Henry's bird

blocks.note: Hal is a pet form of Henry, as with Shakespeare's Prince Hal
a finch is a small songbird

explanation.surface: An instruction to make off with a man's pet bird.
explanation.walkthrough: In Cockney rhyming slang half-inch means pinch, that is, steal.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhyming slang turns pinch into the rhyme half-inch, and to pinch is to steal.

clue.text: I stay and look the other way in Spain and Portugal

indicators.note: facing the other way means pointing backwards, so the word is read from its end

blocks.note: taken as written
to be is to remain, exist
an air is a look or appearance

explanation.surface: A traveller says they stay put and turn their eyes away while in the Iberian countries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'look the other way' reads like ignoring something; only 'look' gives letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Iberian peninsula is the landmass shared by the two nations, so the name covers both.

clue.text: Tina in bra undone was a female warrior

indicators.note: a garment undone has come apart, so the letters fall into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman whose underwear has come loose was once a fighter.
explanation.definitionFit: Britannia, the helmeted figure with trident and shield, personifies Britain as a warrior woman.

clue.text: Metal clip requires hot air power

blocks.note: H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps
taken as written
grip means hold or control

explanation.surface: A metal fastener needs blasts of heated air to work.
explanation.definitionFit: A hairgrip is a small bent metal clip that holds hair in place; Americans call it a bobby pin.

clue.text: Old woman must get her MOT first

indicators.note: first fixes which part is placed at the front of the join

blocks.note: taken as written: the MOT is Britain's annual roadworthiness test for cars
taken as written

explanation.surface: An elderly lady has to take her car for its annual test before anything else.
explanation.walkthrough: Old woman is informal slang for one's mother.
explanation.definitionFit: 'My old woman' is colloquial for a mother, as 'old man' is for father.

clue.text: Phoney dancer

blocks.note: first meaning: a swindler, a dishonest person
second meaning: someone who dances the twist

explanation.walkthrough: Phoney looks like an adjective modifying dancer, but it is a noun for a cheat.
explanation.definitionFit: A twister is a cheat or crook, and also, literally, one who does the 1960s dance the twist.

clue.text: A clam in a dressing could be wild

indicators.note: dressing a salad tosses it about, so these letters are mixed up

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A shellfish in a salad sauce might be untamed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a dressing' reads as a seafood recipe; 'dressing' alone signals the mixing.
explanation.definitionFit: Maniacal means frenzied and crazed, behaving like a maniac, so out of control.

clue.text: Flyer, an aquatic bird biting upturned lip

indicators.note: turned up in a down entry means read from bottom to top
a mouth biting something closes around it

blocks.note: the coot is a black water bird
taken as written

explanation.surface: A flying creature, a water bird, nips a curled lip.
explanation.walkthrough: Flyer suggests the bird; it means a pilot.
explanation.definitionFit: A co-pilot is the second pilot of an aircraft, so one who flies.

clue.text: Head gets above total, which is illegal at cricket

indicators.note: in a down entry, being above means coming first in the join

blocks.note: nob is slang for the head
all means the total amount

explanation.surface: A head teacher scores over the total, which breaks cricket's rules.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a no-ball is an illegal delivery by the bowler, penalised with a run to the batting side.
explanation.definitionFit: The term names a delivery bowled against the rules of cricket, such as overstepping the crease.

clue.text: Binge hour upset the chap next door

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so the letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A late-night drinking session annoyed the man living next door.
explanation.definitionFit: A neighbour is a person who lives nearby, typically in the adjacent house.

clue.text: Try to have time for love

blocks.note: a judge hears, or tries, a case
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Advice to make time for romance.
explanation.walkthrough: Try is the legal sense: to hear a case in court.
explanation.definitionFit: The heart stands for affection by metonymy, as in 'you have my heart'.

clue.text: Savoury jelly is like having endless cream

indicators.note: without an end means the last letter is cut off
having means taking on the next part after it

blocks.note: as means like, in comparison
the cream of something is its pick, the best

explanation.surface: A savoury jelly is compared to a dessert with endless cream.
explanation.definitionFit: Aspic is a clear gelatine made from meat or fish stock, used to set savoury dishes.

clue.text: Shed a tear about ten more

indicators.note: something shed is cast off and scattered, so the letters are thrown into a new order
about means surrounding, so one part is placed round the other

blocks.note: taken as written
X is the Roman numeral for ten

explanation.surface: Someone weeps over ten more of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shed a tear' reads as crying; 'Shed' is the signal and only 'tear' is shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: Extra means additional, beyond what is usual, so more.

clue.text: Anne and I cooked with lard, which increases the blood pressure

indicators.note: cooking transforms ingredients, so these letters are worked into a new form

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Two people fry with pig fat, which is bad for the heart.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a fatty diet raising blood pressure; the definition is a hormone.
explanation.definitionFit: Adrenalin is the hormone released under stress, raising heart rate and blood pressure.

clue.text: Empty talk reduplicated: remember "I" comes before "A"

blocks.note: the answer is a doubled word whose two halves differ only in a vowel
as with chit-chat and tittle-tattle, the half with the I vowel comes first

explanation.surface: A spelling rule-of-thumb about vowel order in repeated words.
explanation.walkthrough: English vowel-change doublets put the I form before the A form, as in zigzag or ping-pong's cousin chit-chat.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means idle chatter, meaningless babble, an old term for trivial talk.
